segments.text: In 2019, Facebook was fined five billion dollars. The largest penalty in FTC history. Eighty-seven million people's data — harvested, profiled, and sold to a political targeting firm without their knowledge. And on the day the fine was announced, Facebook's stock went up. The market added six billion dollars in value. Mark Zuckerberg personally gained one point one billion dollars in a single day. The punishment made the company richer than if the government had done nothing.
segments.notes: Open on news footage of fine announcement. Let 3s of anchor audio ground the viewer in reality before VO takes over. Dollar figure slammed onscreen as static text — no animation, blunt weight.

segments.text: How is that possible?

sfx.motivation: rhetorical hook lands harder in silence — shimmer signals a reframe is coming

segments.notes: 1s pause before the question so the $5B figure breathes. Zuckerberg's face under the klieg lights IS the answer visually. Shimmer SFX underscores the rhetorical pivot.

segments.text: To understand, you need to go back to 1977. Because someone had to discover this trick. And the discovery started with a car on fire.

sfx.motivation: time-jump whoosh cues the viewer we're rewinding to 1977

segments.notes: Dissolve in signals time shift. Whoosh SFX + year card = cinematic rewind. Hosts-at-desk footage stands in for 'experts talking about fines' — abstract enough to not mislead.

segments.text: [CHAPTER: THE FORMULA]

sfx.motivation: chapter punch — single hard impact before silence, per LearnByLeo 5-step chapter transition

segments.notes: Full 5-step chapter transition: (1) impact SFX punch, (2) 0.5s silence, (3) chapter card on dark background, (4) fade out, (5) new energy begins seg 4. Music swells briefly then cuts.

segments.text: In 1977, Ford knew the Pinto's fuel tank ruptured in rear-end collisions. They had the crash test data. Two engineers wrote a cost-benefit analysis — an actual document, with actual numbers. Fix every Pinto: one hundred and thirty-seven million dollars. Expected wrongful death payouts: forty-nine point five million. They shipped the car.
segments.notes: Typewriter reveals 'CRASH TEST DATA, 1977' as VO describes the engineers writing their memo. Dark archival footage + typewriter text sells the documentary authenticity.

segments.text: A thirteen-year-old boy named Richard Grimshaw was a passenger in a Pinto that was rear-ended in San Bernardino. The fuel tank ruptured. The driver burned to death. Richard survived — barely. Burned over his entire body. Lost parts of his fingers. Lost his left ear. Years of skin grafts. A childhood replaced by hospital rooms. The jury awarded one hundred and twenty-five million dollars in punitive damages — the largest in American history. The judge reduced it to three point five million. Ford was acquitted of criminal homicide. No executive went to prison.

sfx.motivation: body impact SFX on burned car image — auditory stand-in for the crash that scarred Grimshaw

segments.notes: 0.5s pause before the boy's name drops — anticipation before the human cost is revealed. Burned car photo is more visceral than clean archival. Lower-third names him immediately.

segments.text: The fine was three point five million dollars. Ford kept selling cars. No one went to prison. And somewhere in a boardroom, someone noticed something. The cost of getting caught was less than the cost of doing the right thing.
segments.notes: DOJ building — the system that extracted $3.5M and called it justice. Fine amount slammed as static text, not animated, because this number should feel obscenely small and inert.

segments.text: That might have been an isolated scandal. A single bad company making a single bad calculation. Except it wasn't.

sfx.motivation: low rumble under 'it wasn't' — signals something much larger is building

segments.notes: Second use of hosts-at-desk — now feels like 'experts cataloguing a pattern' rather than a single case. Rumble SFX on 'Except it wasn't' signals the widening scope.

segments.text: In 2010, a twenty-four-year-old bank teller named Yesenia Guitron did something dangerous. She told the truth. She'd watched her colleagues at Wells Fargo open accounts that customers never asked for — credit cards ordered to addresses that didn't exist, savings accounts funded by moving money between other accounts without permission. She knew why they did it. There was a quota: every customer should have eight products. "Eight is Great." Miss the number and you get a warning. Miss it again and you get fired. So the tellers cheated. Because the alternative was unemployment.
segments.notes: Dissolve in marks the shift to a new case study. Wells Fargo footage grounds us in that institution. Lower-third introduces her as a real person immediately — the human anchor.

segments.text: Yesenia called the company's ethics hotline and reported the fraud. Wells Fargo terminated her the same week. She never found steady work in banking again. Her name went on an industry blacklist — a record that follows you like a scar.

sfx.motivation: impact on the word 'terminated' — the system punishing truth-telling is the shock

segments.notes: Music goes silent as she gets fired — LearnByLeo says silence at emotional peaks hits harder than music. 'TERMINATED' static on screen is brutal and clean.

segments.text: Three point five million fake accounts. Five thousand three hundred tellers fired for opening them. And the woman who designed the quota — Carrie Tolstedt, head of Community Banking — kept fifty-seven million dollars and got zero prison time. She served her sentence at home. Ford's formula required a memo. Wells Fargo's didn't even require a decision — just a number and a threat.
segments.notes: Spreadsheet image while numbers typewrite in — the corporate accounting aesthetic mirrors how Wells Fargo treated the fraud as a line item. Two-line typewriter build creates a data-reveal rhythm.

segments.text: Ford needed a document to do this. Wells Fargo only needed a quota. The next company didn't need either. It just needed a head start.

sfx.motivation: whoosh signals the formula leveling up to its next iteration — 'next company didn't need either'

segments.notes: Boardroom as the locus of the formula — faceless, institutional. Whoosh SFX on 'next company' punctuates each escalation step. Text overlay names what VO is implying.

segments.text: Purdue Pharma saw the lawsuits coming a decade early and withdrew ten point seven billion dollars from the company before anyone could calculate the fine. Richard Sackler promised a, quote, blizzard of prescriptions at OxyContin's launch. In Kermit, West Virginia — population four hundred — a single pharmacy received nine million opioid pills in two years. The pharmacist went to prison. The Sacklers moved their money. More than eight hundred thousand Americans died. The settlement: seven point four billion. The family's remaining fortune: thirteen billion. Nine thousand dollars per death. Ford valued a life at two hundred thousand in 1977. The Sacklers got it down to nine thousand.

sfx.motivation: deep rumble under '$10.7 billion withdrawn' — this number is almost incomprehensible, the rumble conveys dread

segments.notes: Purdue documentary footage. The number on screen is the thesis made concrete — they saw the lawsuits coming and emptied the vault. Rumble plays under 'decade early' for maximum dread.

segments.text: [PAUSE]
segments.notes: This is the [PAUSE] segment. 3 full seconds of silence on a DOJ settlement document — the viewer sits with Ford, Wells Fargo, Purdue. Music silent. No text. Let the weight accumulate before the thesis lands.

segments.text: The fine is cheaper than the profit. Every time. Without exception.

sfx.motivation: hard impact as the thesis drops — 'every time, without exception' is the reveal

segments.notes: Stay on the settlement document — the visual IS the argument. Impact SFX as the absolute ('Without exception') lands. Keep music silent so the words hit air. Text confirms what VO says.

segments.text: The law doesn't prevent corporate crime. It prices it.

sfx.motivation: glass shatter is the thesis line shattering the myth of the law as deterrent — the single most important SFX in the video

segments.text: And the price keeps dropping. Since 2000, corporations have paid over one trillion dollars in fines and settlements in the United States alone. One hundred and twenty-seven companies have each paid more than a billion. And here's the number that should end every argument about whether the system works: companies caught repeatedly pay smaller fines as a percentage of their revenue over time. Not larger. Smaller. The more you violate, the better the deal gets.
segments.notes: Wall Street trading floor = where the math is done. Trillion-dollar figure typewriting in creates a data-reveal moment after the thesis. Music resumes quietly as we move from revelation into evidence.

segments.text: Each company added one feature to the original calculation. Ford added a memo. Wells Fargo added plausible deniability. Purdue added preemption. Facebook added scale. But every one of them had something in common — the damage, at least in theory, could be reversed. Ford could recall the car. Wells Fargo could close the accounts. Purdue could stop making the pills.
segments.notes: Second boardroom use — now it IS the formula being named. VO recapping each company's 'feature' as the camera watches faceless executives. Static 'THE FORMULA' text underscores the systemic nature.

segments.text: Then the formula met the internet. And the damage became permanent.

sfx.motivation: whoosh signals the pivot to the digital era — the formula jumping to internet scale

segments.notes: Dissolve into server corridors — we're entering the digital era. Whoosh + text card functions as a mini-pivot before the chapter transition. Music shifts to signal new chapter energy incoming.

segments.text: [CHAPTER: THE DATA]

sfx.motivation: chapter punch — impact before silence in the 5-step chapter transition

segments.notes: 5-step chapter transition: (1) impact SFX, (2) 0.5s silence, (3) THE DATA chapter card on dark server background, (4) fade to black, (5) new energy at seg 21. Slightly lower tension reset before Facebook arc climbs again.

segments.text: Facebook was the bridge between the old formula and the new one.
segments.notes: Return to Facebook footage — we're back where we started but now we understand WHY. Lower-third 'The Bridge' signals to viewers that this isn't recap, it's the connective tissue. New chapter energy, slightly calmer before the Cambridge Analytica details escalate.

segments.text: In 2013, a Cambridge University researcher named Aleksandr Kogan built a personality quiz app. Two hundred and seventy thousand people downloaded it. But Facebook's API — the system that connects apps to the platform — gave the quiz access to not just those users' data, but all of their friends' data too. Every like, every post, every photo, every connection. Two hundred and seventy thousand downloads became eighty-seven million people's data harvested in weeks.

sfx.motivation: typewriter SFX as data accumulates — 270K becomes 87M, the sound of scale being logged

segments.notes: Phone with Facebook app is the 'innocent object' that became a data weapon. Typewriter SFX as the numbers typewrite in — each digit of 87,000,000 landing with a keystroke. The gap between 270K and 87M should feel obscene.

segments.text: Facebook knew this was possible. It was a feature, not a bug — they'd designed the API to be open because open APIs drive engagement, and engagement drives advertising revenue. In 2014, they quietly changed the rules. But they never enforced deletion of the data already taken.

sfx.motivation: shimmer on 'feature, not a bug' — sounds like a realization crystallizing, which is what this moment IS

segments.notes: Server corridors — the infrastructure of the intentional design. Shimmer SFX on the reframe moment. 'FEATURE. NOT BUG.' as static text is a deliberate callback to tech industry language weaponized against users.

segments.text: Cambridge Analytica used that data to build voter profiles so precise they could predict what would make you angry before you felt it. They were hired by the Trump campaign. They were hired by groups supporting Brexit.
segments.text_overlay:
VOTER PROFILES
Built from your personality
segments.notes: Cambridge Analytica documentary footage is the ideal B-roll for this specific claim. Lower-third names what the profiles were FOR — voter manipulation — before VO makes it explicit.

segments.text: Eighty-seven million people's personalities — measured, modeled, and weaponized — for the price of a free quiz they never took. And most of them still don't know. A 2019 Pew survey found that seventy-four percent of Facebook users didn't know the platform maintained a list of their interests and traits for ad targeting. They didn't know they'd been profiled. They didn't know their data had been sold. They just knew that their feed felt different in 2016 — angrier, more anxious, more polarized — and they assumed that was the world changing. It wasn't the world. It was the algorithm. Tuned by their own data, sold without their consent, deployed to shape an election.

sfx.motivation: impact on 'weaponized' — the word is the reveal, the SFX confirms the horror

segments.notes: 0.5s pause before 'weaponized' — LearnByLeo anticipation rule. Music goes silent as the human scale of 87M hits. Data center image recontextualizes: the server corridors aren't infrastructure, they're the crime scene. Number on screen in cold white text.

segments.text: When the story broke in March 2018, Zuckerberg was summoned before Congress. He wore a suit. He said sorry. And then something happened that tells you everything about why the formula survives.
segments.notes: Dissolve into hearing — signals time jump to the Congressional moment. 2s of hearing room ambient audio (murmur, clicks) before VO takes over gives the viewer the space of a real room. Lower-third dates it.

segments.text: A United States senator — a person with the power to regulate the most valuable company on Earth — looked at Mark Zuckerberg and asked: "How does Facebook make money if the product is free?"

sfx.motivation: low rumble under the description of a senator's power — the institution IS the stakes

segments.notes: Capitol building as the visual embodiment of 'person with the power to regulate.' Rumble SFX underscores the gravity of what's about to NOT happen. Wideshot — institutional scale against one man.

segments.text: Zuckerberg paused. And said: "Senator, we run ads."

sfx.motivation: shimmer just before the line drops — the crystallization of the entire video's thesis into four words

segments.notes: 1.5s pause before the line — maximum anticipation. Shimmer SFX. Then 4s of actual hearing audio if Zuckerberg's voice/pause is audible. Quote text appears the moment he says it. Close on face — the smug calm IS the formula personified. Music stays silent. This line is the second thesis of the video.

segments.text: The room laughed. The internet turned it into a meme. For weeks, the clip circulated as comedy — an old senator, a young CEO, a punchline about boomers not understanding technology.
segments.notes: Dissolve out signals the ironic deflation — the room laughed, the internet made it a meme, nothing changed. Cambridge Analytica footage as B-roll for 'the internet circulated it' fits thematically. Music resumes — the machine keeps running. Tension drops to 0.55: the aftermath of a moment that should have been a reckoning but wasn't.

segments.text: And it was funny. It genuinely was. The man in charge of regulating the most valuable company on Earth didn't know how it made money. That's objectively absurd. It's the kind of thing you'd write into a satire and worry it was too on the nose.
segments.notes: Zuckerberg hearing is the perfect visual anchor. Brief clip audio establishes atmosphere, then mute under VO. Face zoom on the man who didn't know how the internet worked.

segments.text: [PAUSE]

sfx.motivation: pause beat — shimmer signals the reframe about to happen

segments.notes: This IS the pause segment. Hold on Zuckerberg photo, 2s silence. Shimmer SFX signals a perspective shift incoming. Anticipation before the reframe.

segments.text: But here's what nobody said at the time. That hearing was the formula protecting itself. The people who set the fines — who write the regulations, who are supposed to be the ceiling on corporate behavior — didn't understand the business model of the company they were interrogating. And Zuckerberg knew it. He sat there, patient and composed, and explained his own business to the people who were supposed to be punishing him. He wasn't being grilled. He was giving a tutorial. And everyone watched it happen and laughed — because it was easier to laugh than to realize what it meant.

sfx.motivation: the formula protecting itself — needs weight and foreboding

segments.notes: Capitol exterior reframes the hearing — the system regulating itself. Rumble SFX + lower third crystallizes the thesis. Wide shot conveys institutional scale.

segments.text: The people who set the fines don't understand what they're fining. The companies being fined have always known that.
segments.notes: Two men discussing fines is a literal visual for 'people who set fines don't understand what they're fining.' Unintentional irony is the editorial joke. No SFX — let the image work.

segments.text: The FTC investigated for over a year. In July 2019, they announced the largest fine in their history: five billion dollars.
segments.notes: FTC official at podium — clip audio for credibility ('This settlement is the result of an exhaustive investigation') then mute. Official tone before we undercut it with the 7% stat.

segments.text: Here is what five billion dollars means to Facebook. Revenue that year: seventy point seven billion. The fine was seven percent. Net profit: eighteen point five billion. The fine was about twenty-seven percent of one year's profit — paid once, for a violation that ran for years and compromised eighty-seven million people.

sfx.motivation: $5B = 7% of revenue — this stat is the gut punch, needs a hit

segments.notes: Spreadsheet close-up grounds the abstraction in financial reality. Impact SFX + static text makes the percentage land. Static over typewriter — this is a calculated figure, not a breaking story.

segments.text: The FTC vote was three to two. Party line. The two dissenting commissioners didn't think the fine was too harsh. They thought it was too lenient. They wanted to sue, not settle. They wanted to hold Zuckerberg personally liable. They lost.
segments.notes: Second Facebook clip for the partisan vote detail. Lower third shows 3-2 split. The kicker — dissenters thought it was too SMALL — pays off the viewer who reads the overlay.

segments.text: On July twelfth, when the fine amount leaked, Facebook's stock rose one percent. The market had expected worse. Investors were relieved. Mark Zuckerberg's net worth increased by one point one billion dollars that day. He made more from the announcement of the fine than the fine cost the company. The market's verdict was clear: this is the ceiling. This is the worst it gets. And the worst it gets is a good day.

sfx.motivation: stock rising on a $5B fine is the perverse punchline — impact punctuates the absurdity

segments.notes: Wall Street floor for the stock rally reveal. 1s pause before for LearnByLeo anticipation. Impact SFX on the stat. Music rises briefly — the market literally celebrated. Wide shot for institutional scope.

segments.text: Now. After everything I've just shown you — Ford, Wells Fargo, Purdue, Facebook — you'd be forgiven for thinking the formula is unbeatable. That this is just how it works. Fine, settle, move on. Nobody learns. Nothing changes.
segments.notes: Gavel dissolve signals the transition to the 'what if' pivot. Lower energy after the stock reveal — the system worked exactly as designed. Dissolve slows us down before the GDPR reframe.

segments.text: But something happened in 2023 that proves the formula can break.

sfx.motivation: something changed — shimmer signals new information entering

segments.notes: GDPR document signals the European legal shift. 1.5s pause for anticipation before the pivot. Shimmer + lower third sets up the counterexample cleanly.

segments.text: Ireland fined Meta one point two billion euros under Europe's GDPR — a law that scales fines to four percent of global annual revenue. Not a negotiated number. Not a fixed ceiling. A percentage.
segments.notes: Ireland fine announcement clip. Brief clip audio for news credibility. Static text shows the number prominently. The 4% of global revenue mechanic is the key — it scales with size.

segments.text: And Facebook — the same Facebook that turned a five-billion-dollar American fine into a stock rally — panicked.

sfx.motivation: Facebook PANICKED is the reveal — needs a hit before the explanation

segments.notes: Callback to Zuckerberg face — the man who was unflappable in Senate now has the company panicking. Impact SFX + bold 'PANICKED' text overlay. The contrast with the hearing is the editorial point.

segments.text: Within weeks, they rewrote their entire data transfer infrastructure. They shut down a pipeline they'd run for a decade. They rebuilt their European architecture from scratch. They didn't fight it in court for years. They didn't issue a press release and wait for it to blow over. They fixed it. Immediately. Because for the first time, the violation was more expensive than the profit.
segments.notes: Symmetrical server corridor for 'rewrote their entire data transfer infrastructure.' The physical scale of what they were forced to dismantle hits differently when you understand the stakes. No SFX — image carries it.

segments.text: Sit with that for a second. The formula — the one that has survived five decades, across every industry, through every administration — broke. In Europe. Because someone changed one variable: they made the fine proportional.
segments.notes: Handwritten math formulas for 'the formula survived five decades.' The formula IS math — literalizing the metaphor visually. No SFX, no text — let the narration breathe.

segments.text: Same company. Same executives. Same data. The only difference was the math. And when the math changed, the behavior changed overnight.
segments.text_overlay: SAME COMPANY. SAME DATA. DIFFERENT MATH.
segments.notes: Second data center angle for 'same company, same data' — the visual rhyme reinforces the point. Static text overlay drives home the thesis. The only variable that changed was the fine math.

segments.text: So at this point in the story, you might be thinking: okay, the formula exists, but there are limits. Europe found the off switch. Proportional fines work. The system can be fixed. Companies can be forced to change. Maybe — just maybe — we're figuring it out.

segments.text: Here's a thought experiment. What if you could take anything you wanted from anyone — their writing, their art, their music, their photographs, their private conversations — and the only consequence was paying a fraction of what it was worth, years after you'd already used it to build a product worth billions?
segments.notes: Digital artist at work for the thought experiment — 'their writing, their art, their music.' This is the physical act of creation being described. Present tense, human scale.

segments.text: You'd take everything. Obviously. Everyone would.
segments.notes: Abstract gavel image + 'YOU'D TAKE EVERYTHING' bold static overlay. Short sentence needs punchy visual. Text is doing the heavy lifting here — four words that indict the viewer before the indict.

segments.text: That's not a thought experiment. That's the AI industry's business model.

sfx.motivation: central thesis reveal of the AI section — deserves a hit

segments.text: In October 2025, a Reddit engineer did something clever. They created a post — ordinary-looking, about a fictional company — and made it visible only through Google's search index. You couldn't find it by browsing Reddit. You couldn't stumble on it. The only way to reach it was through a crawler. It was bait. A tripwire designed to catch one thing: an AI company scraping Reddit's content without permission.
segments.notes: Reddit browsing for the honeypot story setup. Familiar site establishes normalcy before the trap. No SFX — narrative buildup needs clean pacing. The ordinary precedes the clever.

segments.text: Within hours, Perplexity AI cited the post. Word for word.

segments.text: But it's not arrogance. It's arithmetic. They did the math. The data was worth more than any fine. The model being trained on that data was worth more than any lawsuit. And once the data is inside the model —

segments.text: When Ford got caught, they could recall the car. When Facebook got caught, they could — in theory — delete the data. When Purdue got caught, they could stop manufacturing the pills. The damage was reversible. Expensive, slow, and nobody ever did it voluntarily. But the off switch existed.
segments.notes: Ford/Facebook/AI comparison — Cambridge Analytica grounds the Facebook data scandal visually. VO carries the tri-part argument. Mute clip audio. Energy deliberately pulls back from seg 1 to let the analogy breathe.

segments.text: With AI, there is no off switch. When a model trains on scraped data, that data dissolves into the model's parameters like sugar dissolved in water. You cannot un-dissolve it. You cannot identify which outputs came from which inputs. You cannot point to a sentence and say "that came from Reddit" or "that came from a children's book published in 2019." The data becomes the model. The violation becomes the product. Every response the AI generates, every image it creates, every answer it provides — built on content taken without permission and impossible to return.

sfx.motivation: subsonic machine rumble under 'no off switch' — the physical reality of unstoppable infrastructure

segments.notes: Data center corridors = the physical body of AI. Static text overlay 'No off switch.' lands the thesis as a visual anchor. Rumble builds under the revelation that training is permanent.

segments.text: Even if every AI company loses every lawsuit, they keep the models. The models keep running. The products keep generating revenue. The fine doesn't undo the training. It just pays for the data after the fact — like shoplifting and mailing a check later. Except the check is always less than the retail price.
segments.notes: Even if every lawsuit is won — models keep running. Still image of server hall with slow zoom gives cold, mechanical dread. No SFX, let VO carry the inevitability argument without competition.

segments.text: And the people who try to stop it? Remember Yesenia Guitron — the Wells Fargo teller who called the ethics hotline and was fired for it? The formula punishes the people who resist it. It rewards the people who run it. That pattern repeats in every industry, in every decade.

segments.text: I want to tell you about Elliana Esquivel. Because her story is the one that makes this real — and the one that shows you how the formula works when it's happening to a person, not a company.

sfx.motivation: soft shimmer introduces Elliana — intimate, delicate, a life before it was taken

segments.notes: Introduce Elliana with warmth before the devastation arrives. Half-beat pause per LearnByLeo anticipation rule. Lower-third name card. Shimmer is gentle, aspirational — her life before the scrape. Dissolve in signals new character energy.

segments.text: Elliana is an illustrator in Charlotte, North Carolina. Self-taught. She spent years building a career in minimalistic line work — psychological, introspective, distinctive. The kind of art you'd recognize on a bookshelf. She illustrated covers for HarperCollins, Little Brown, and Faber and Faber. She designed album art for Universal Music Group. She created promotional work for Hulu. Art was her full-time job for four years. She'd built something.
segments.notes: Continue building Elliana's world — show her at work building her portfolio. Different start point for visual variety (second use). Location lower-third grounds the character geographically. No SFX, let the VO paint the picture.

segments.text: Then she visited a website called Have I Been Trained. It's a tool that lets creators check whether their work was scraped into the LAION-5B dataset — the five-billion-image training set used by Stability AI's Stable Diffusion and other image generators.

sfx.motivation: whoosh on 'Have I Been Trained' — the tool that revealed the violation, sudden discovery energy

segments.notes: The moment of discovery. Typewriter text of the website name creates a documentary identification effect. Whoosh signals entry into new territory. Half-beat pause before the revelation that everything is in there.

segments.text: Almost her entire portfolio was in there.

sfx.motivation: impact hit on 'almost her entire portfolio' — the gut punch of violation

segments.notes: 1-second pause before this line — maximum LearnByLeo anticipation before the reveal. Impact SFX on the cut. Large static text overlay echoes and amplifies the VO. The gavel image reinforces the legal/theft framing subliminally.

segments.text: Every illustration she'd spent months creating. Every piece that defined her style. Scraped, indexed, and fed into a model that anyone could now use to generate images that look like her work — for free. A publisher she'd worked with for two years emailed to say they were "exploring AI-generated options" for their next cover. Her commissions dropped. Her online sales fell. The style she'd spent a decade developing could now be approximated in seconds by typing a sentence into a box. She started pivoting to 3D art — not because she wanted to, but because she hoped three-dimensional work would be harder to scrape.

sfx.motivation: heavy body impact on 'scraped, indexed, and fed' — visceral physical metaphor for consumption

segments.notes: Peak violation moment — years of work consumed. Body impact SFX is deliberately physical; 'fed into a model' has the undertone of ingestion, violence. No text overlay — let the VO carry full weight without distraction.

segments.text: When someone asked her about getting her work removed from the dataset, she said it was pointless. Quote: "It'll just get scraped again, and it'll end up back on the website." She called it, quote, a dystopian thing to be dealing with.
segments.notes: Elliana's quote is the emotional apex of her arc. Typewriter reveal of her exact words while showing the artist at work creates devastating dissonance. Third and final use of the clip at a new start point. No SFX — the quote stands alone.

segments.text: Elliana isn't suing anyone. She can't afford to. Over seventy copyright lawsuits are active against AI companies as of March 2026 — Anthropic settled for one point five billion, OpenAI is fighting the New York Times, and not one company has slowed down. The largest settlement in history paid out roughly three thousand dollars per stolen work.
segments.notes: Energy deliberately settles — Elliana cannot afford to fight, but 70+ others are trying. Gavel clip grounds the legal dimension. Static stat overlay widens the lens from one person to a movement. Aftermath beat lets the audience process.

segments.text: Three thousand dollars. That's what Elliana's illustrations are worth in this market — years of work, commissions for HarperCollins, Universal Music, Hulu — priced at the same rate as a single scraped novel. If the class-action settlement arrives, her share might cover a month of rent. The model keeps generating images in her style. The violation is the product. The fine — if it ever arrives — is a fraction of what her career was worth.

sfx.motivation: impact on the $3,000 figure — years of work reduced to an absurdly small number

segments.notes: The $3,000 is the killer stat for this character arc. Large static text overlay. Half-beat pause for anticipation. Impact SFX before the number. Chart/graph image reinforces the reductive logic of market pricing applied to human creative work.

segments.text: And this brings us to you. Because if you've ever posted on Reddit, commented on YouTube, written a blog, tweeted, left a review, uploaded a photo, published anything anywhere on the open internet — your content is in training datasets right now. Not hypothetically. Provably. Common Crawl, the dataset most large language models train on, contains over two hundred and fifty billion web pages. Your words are in there. The companies building hundred-billion-dollar products on your words did not ask your permission.

sfx.motivation: whoosh on the direct viewer address — pulls the audience into the story personally

segments.notes: The 'this brings us to you' turn is the video's personal stake pivot. Half-beat pause per LearnByLeo. Typewriter 'This is about you.' makes it impossible to ignore. Music begins rising to signal the argument is escalating toward a conclusion.

segments.text: Ford's formula was clumsy — a memo with signatures. Wells Fargo's was structural — a quota with plausible deniability. Purdue's was preemptive — move the money before the fine. Facebook's was mathematical — the fine is smaller than the profit.
segments.notes: The formula comparison — Ford clumsy, WF structural, AI irreversible. Talking-head clip grounds the 'cost of doing business' framing analytically. Music ducks under VO. This segment is expository — visual supports without distracting.

segments.text: AI's formula is all of those things. Plus one more: irreversible. Scrape now. Train the model. Make it indispensable. Settle later. The model can't be untrained. The fine is just the cost of raw materials, paid after the factory is already built and too valuable to demolish.

sfx.motivation: subsonic rumble under 'irreversible' — the word that defines AI's formula over all others

segments.notes: Final word before chapter transition. All-caps static IRREVERSIBLE. Rumble underscores permanence. Half-beat tail after the word. Fade to black sets up the chapter card cleanly — LearnByLeo chapter transition step 1.

segments.text: [CHAPTER: THE RENT]

sfx.motivation: punch whoosh on chapter card — step 1 of LearnByLeo 5-step chapter transition

segments.notes: Full LearnByLeo 5-step chapter transition: (1) whoosh punch from previous fade-to-black, (2) 2s silence with fade-from-black, (3) chapter card THE RENT, (4) housing crisis footage as new energy, (5) hook into Chris Vialpondo. Music bridges the sections.

segments.text: Ford paid three point five million. Wells Fargo paid three billion. Purdue paid seven point four billion. Facebook paid five billion. Those numbers got bigger — but so did the profits. The ratio never changed. The fine was always less than the take.
segments.notes: Escalating fine sequence is a data moment. Financial spreadsheet image grounds the corporate accounting logic. Typewriter reveals the fine progression — the numbers arriving one by one create visual drama out of raw figures.

segments.text: So what happens when the formula reaches its logical conclusion? What happens when the fine is zero?

sfx.motivation: low rumble building under the rhetorical question — dread, not resolution

segments.text_overlay: What if the fine is zero?
segments.notes: 1-second pause before the central rhetorical question of the chapter — maximum anticipation. Typewriter question on settlement image. Rumble builds underneath. The question is left hanging intentionally — the answer comes at seg 27.

segments.text: Chris Vialpondo is a renter in Seattle's Lower Queen Anne neighborhood. In 2022, he opened a notice from his property manager and learned his rent had increased by fifty percent. Same apartment. Same neighborhood. Same job. He was already working two jobs to make rent. Fifty percent meant the difference between getting by and going under. It meant counting every grocery trip. It meant the constant math of which bill gets paid this week and which one waits. He reached out to his property manager — the human being he thought had set the price — and was told nothing could be done. Because his property manager hadn't set the price. A company he'd never heard of had.
segments.notes: Ground Chris Vialpondo in his neighborhood with an aerial shot — place him in the world before the violation. Lower-third introduces the character. Half-beat pause before the personal story. Establish intimacy before the outrage.

segments.text: RealPage. A company that takes confidential pricing data from competing landlords — data that competitors are not legally supposed to share — and feeds it into an algorithm that recommends rent prices across more than thirteen million apartments. Ninety percent of landlords follow the recommendation. The result: coordinated rent increases across buildings that are supposed to be competing with each other. The Department of Justice found that the algorithm costs renters an average of seventy dollars a month more — and over a hundred dollars a month in six major metro areas.

sfx.motivation: heavy impact on 'RealPage' — villain reveal, corporate name landing like an indictment

segments.notes: Villain reveal. Play 4 seconds of clip audio (investigators speaking) — the actual documentary voice adds authenticity — then mute under VO. Heavy impact SFX. Typewriter text of company name frames them as defendant. Half-beat pause for anticipation.

segments.text: Chris spoke publicly at the Washington state attorney general's press conference. He said: "The most painful and revolting part about all of it is that all of the money I spent unnecessarily is now in the pockets of those who need it the least."
segments.notes: Peak emotional tension of the chapter — Chris's direct quote. Typewriter reveal of his opening words creates a documentary quote card effect while housing footage maintains visual context. Second use of the clip at a new start point.

segments.text: The DOJ sued and announced a settlement in November 2025. RealPage has to modify its software. Landlords have to be allowed to set prices below the algorithm's floor. No fine. No compensation to renters. No admission of guilt.
segments.notes: Energy deliberately drops — settlement announcement. DOJ building provides institutional gravitas and false resolution before the $0 reveal. Lower-third timestamps the event. No SFX — institutional silence before the gut punch of seg 27.

segments.text: To be clear: a company was found to have coordinated rent prices for millions of apartments, and the settlement was essentially "please update your software." If you got caught fixing prices at a farmers' market, you'd face harsher consequences. Eight hundred thousand leases in Washington alone were priced by the algorithm.

sfx.motivation: glass shatter on '$0' — the fine that shatters the entire concept of legal accountability

segments.notes: The chapter's killer stat. 1.5s pause before the reveal — longest pause yet, maximum anticipation. Music drops to complete silence. Glass shatter SFX. Large static '$0' on screen. This answers the rhetorical question posed in seg 22. The settlement image used again grounds the irony.

segments.text: And after getting caught fixing rent for millions of people, RealPage's first move was to sue the state of New York for passing a law that banned algorithmic rent-setting.

sfx.motivation: whoosh on the audacity pivot — RealPage suing the state it victimized

segments.notes: The audacity of suing the state that tried to hold them accountable demands a whoosh and typewriter text to let the irony detonate. NY State Capitol grounds the counter-attack geographically. Music begins rising — building to the final chapter beat.

segments.text: And then RealPage did something that tells you everything about how the formula works when it's fully internalized. New York State passed a law banning algorithmic rent-setting — the first state to say, explicitly, that this practice is illegal. RealPage's response was not to comply. Not to modify their business. They sued New York. The company that was just caught coordinating rent prices for millions of people went to court to argue that the state didn't have the right to stop them.

sfx.motivation: final impact — the formula fully internalized, no shame, no retreat, no reckoning

segments.notes: Closing beat of the chapter. Corporate boardroom is the formula's natural habitat. Half-beat pause before, 1.5s tail after to let the impact land. Typewriter text echoes the thesis. Impact SFX. Fade to black signals the end of this chapter arc and the transition to what comes next.

segments.text: That's not a company that got caught and feels chastened. That's a company that did the math and concluded — correctly, so far — that the system will let them continue.

segments.text: [CHAPTER: THE RECKONING]

sfx.motivation: chapter card punch — LearnByLeo 5-step opener: punch before the card

segments.text: Europe figured this out. Four percent of global revenue. Proportional. Automatic. No ceiling. When the fine scales with the company, the formula breaks. Facebook shrugged off a five-billion-dollar American fine and panicked over a European one. The tools exist. Criminal liability for executives — not the tellers, the architects. Disgorgement — hand back every dollar earned from the violation, not a negotiated fraction. The legal frameworks are built. The question has never been how. The question is why.

sfx.motivation: shimmer on 'Europe figured this out' — rare moment of functional governance, a glimmer

segments.notes: Energy deliberately resets post-chapter-card. European Parliament chamber shows governance that actually works — a contrast to everything just documented. Shimmer = rare positive note. Typewriter text emphasizes the proportional penalty as narrator says it.

segments.text: And the answer is the same math that runs everything else in this video. The companies that benefit from the formula fund the campaigns, staff the advisory boards, draft the legislation. The fine stays small because the people who pay it set the ceiling.

segments.text: Richard Grimshaw survived the Pinto fire. He grew up carrying scars that covered his body and a verdict that was supposed to change things — one hundred and twenty-five million dollars, reduced to three point five million. The message was: we've done the math, and your pain has a price. Ford paid it and moved on.

segments.text: Yesenia Guitron called the ethics hotline and was fired for it. She never worked in banking again. Carrie Tolstedt, who built the quota system, kept fifty-seven million dollars.

segments.text: The Sackler name is still on a wing of the Guggenheim Museum in New York City. The Metropolitan Museum took theirs down after public outcry. The Guggenheim hasn't. You can walk into one of the most prestigious cultural institutions in the world, look up at the wall, and read the name of a family that earned their fortune from a drug that killed eight hundred thousand people. They kept thirteen billion. And they kept the wall.
segments.notes: New York institution — close enough to the Guggenheim context. Typewriter text on 'THE SACKLER NAME' makes it feel engraved, permanent. No SFX — quiet outrage works better here. The Met took theirs down. The Guggenheim didn't. That gap is the story.

segments.text: That's the formula. It even gets you a plaque.

segments.text: The Grush-Saunby memo put a dollar value on a human life in 1977. Two hundred thousand dollars. Purdue's settlement valued each opioid death at nine thousand. Facebook's fine valued each compromised user at fifty-seven dollars. The AI settlements value each stolen book at three thousand dollars. Elliana's illustrations? Not priced yet. Your Reddit posts? Your YouTube comments? Your blog from 2016?
